options.B: Path normalization and Unicode/encoding ambiguities to defeat naive path-based ACLs
options.C: Reflected XSS payloads that execute in the admin console
options.D: Clickjacking against the admin interface to trick a user into navigation

explanation: This is a path canonicalization/normalization failure: double-encoding, dot-segment tricks, and Unicode homoglyphs can cause the gateway and the upstream service to interpret the path differently, bypassing prefix filters (B). Wordlists (A) don’t explain evading a block with encoded/Unicode variants. XSS (C) is orthogonal to access control decisions. Clickjacking (D) abuses UI framing, not server-side path checks. Robust defenses canonicalize/normalize before policy checks, use allowlists mapped to resolved routes, and test with double-encoding/Unicode variants.

question: You are hardening credential storage after a breach exposed a database of unsalted SHA-1 password hashes. Which change MOST effectively counters offline cracking and rainbow tables going forward?

options.A: Enforce 12-character minimums and complexity rules only
options.B: Encrypt the hash table with AES-256-GCM at rest and keep using SHA-1 for hashing
options.C: Salt with a single global “pepper” value and keep a fast hash for performance
options.D: Store passwords using Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt or PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 with a unique per-user salt and tuned cost (iterations/memory); optionally add an application-level pepper in an HSM

explanation: Rainbow tables exploit unsalted, fast hashes. The proper countermeasure is a unique per-user salt plus a slow (preferably memory-hard) KDF such as Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt (or PBKDF2 with high iterations), optionally adding a pepper stored separately (e.g., HSM), so D is correct. A improves entropy but does not defeat fast offline cracking. B protects data at rest only; once read, fast SHA-1 remains weak. C a single “pepper” alone does not replace per-user salts or slow KDFs.

question: A Java-based e-commerce site stores a Base64-encoded session cookie that, when decoded, contains a serialized object. Modifying the payload to a known gadget chain results in remote code execution on a vulnerable library version. What web application threat BEST explains this issue?

options.A: XML external entity (XXE) processing in the login response
options.B: SQL injection via unsafe deserialization of string fields
options.C: Insecure deserialization leading to arbitrary code execution
options.D: Server-side template injection (SSTI) via EL expressions in JSP

explanation: Insecure deserialization occurs when untrusted serialized data is accepted and deserialized, allowing attackers to supply gadget chains that trigger dangerous behavior up to RCE; the Base64 cookie containing a serialized object is a hallmark. XXE (A) involves XML parser misconfiguration and external entities, not object streams. SQL injection (B) is about injecting SQL into database queries; while deserialized data may later reach a DB, the described RCE via gadget chains is characteristic of insecure deserialization. SSTI (D) affects template engines (e.g., Freemarker, Thymeleaf, Velocity), whereas the scenario centers on Java object deserialization. Mitigations include avoiding native deserialization for untrusted data, using signed/crypto-MAC’d tokens with strict verification, employing allowlisted transformers, and upgrading libraries to remove known gadget chains.

question: During red-team testing you discover that internal hosts are exfiltrating via DNS tunneling. Which set of countermeasures MOST effectively detects and disrupts DNS-based covert channels?

options.A: Apply DNS egress filtering (force use of enterprise resolvers), limit permitted query types, enforce length/label limits, apply entropy and volume detection, and use RPZ/secure DNS policies.
options.B: Block ICMP and UDP everywhere.
options.C: Disable DNS entirely on all hosts and rely only on hard-coded IPs.
options.D: Only use static threat feeds for known malicious domains and ignore behavior.

explanation: A is correct because DNS tunneling is best mitigated by layered DNS controls: force internal clients to use controlled resolvers, block external recursive resolvers, limit allowed record types (e.g., TXT), monitor query volume, label length and entropy (base32/base64 indicators), and apply RPZ/Threat Intel to block known malicious zones. B is overbroad and disruptive (DNS uses UDP). C is untenable operationally. D is insufficient because tunneling uses new/legitimate-looking domains and behavior-based detection is required.

question: Which open-source tool is purpose-built to automate detection, fingerprinting, exploitation and (when authorized) data extraction for SQL injection across many DBMSs, and includes features such as multiple technique selection (--technique), tamper scripts, DBMS fingerprinting (--dbms), and OOB (DNS/HTTP) callbacks?

options.A: sqlmap
options.B: Burp Repeater
options.C: Wireshark
options.D: Nikto

explanation: sqlmap is the specialist automation tool for SQL injection: it enumerates injection points, fingerprints DBMS types/versions, supports techniques (boolean, time, error, UNION, stacked), allows tamper scripts to modify payloads, and supports OOB channels (DNS/HTTP) for exfiltration. Burp Repeater (B) is a manual request replay/modify tool useful for controlled probes but not a full automation/exploitation framework. Wireshark (C) is a packet capture tool and does not perform SQLi testing; it may be useful for observing network activity but not for injection payload crafting. Nikto (D) is a web server/vulnerability scanner focused on misconfigurations and common vulnerabilities, not a dedicated SQLi exploitation framework. In CEHv13 methodology, use sqlmap for automated enumeration only after manual confirmation and within scope.

question: A user opens an emailed Excel file that contains “Enable Content” prompts. Security logs show excel.exe spawning cmd.exe which launches powershell.exe to download and execute a Trojan from a cloud bucket. You want to stop this class of infection without disabling macros organization-wide. Which single control is MOST targeted to this technique?

options.A: Require PowerShell Constrained Language Mode and script signing only
options.B: Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rule: “Block all Office applications from creating child processes”
options.C: Block TCP/443 egress for all endpoints except the security team
options.D: Disable SMBv1 and NetBIOS over TCP/IP on workstations

explanation: The ASR rule blocking Office child processes (B) directly prevents the macro-to-cmd/powershell process chain that Trojans leverage (ATT&CK: T1204, T1059). Constrained Language Mode/signing (A) is valuable but can be bypassed (e.g., unmanaged interpreters, living-off-the-land binaries) and does not stop Office from spawning them. Blanket 443 egress blocks (C) are operationally impractical and overbroad while still leaving other paths (e.g., proxies) unless finely tuned. Disabling SMBv1/NetBIOS (D) hardens lateral movement, not initial macro spawning. CEH recommends ASR/AppLocker/WDAC plus mail and content filtering for Trojan macro pathways.

question: Which search-engine operator combination is MOST useful for discovering sensitive configuration files (e.g., .env, .git/config) that have been accidentally exposed on web servers?

options.A: site:target.com inurl:.git
options.B: site:target.com intitle:"login"
options.C: site:target.com filetype:log
options.D: site:target.com intext:"API_KEY="

explanation: site:target.com inurl:.git targets URLs containing .git, often exposing .git directories that may be publicly accessible and allow download of repository objects and configuration files (including .git/config), a commonly exploited misconfiguration. This dork is widely used in reconnaissance to identify inadvertently exposed repositories. Option B (intitle:"login") identifies login pages but not exposed config files. Option C (filetype:log) can find logs but many servers don't index raw logs and it’s less precise. Option D (intext:"API_KEY=") could find pages where keys are printed, but it relies on the site exposing key strings verbatim and may return fewer actionable hits than .git exposure.

question: Which of the following attacker capabilities made the Kaminsky-style DNS cache poisoning attacks (2008) significantly easier and more reliable against many resolvers at the time?

options.A: Use of DNSSEC validation failures on authoritative servers
options.B: Predictability (or low entropy) of source UDP port and DNS transaction ID on many resolvers
options.C: The prevalence of IPv6-only resolvers without fallback
options.D: Weak TLS certificate validation on authoritative nameservers

explanation: The Kaminsky vulnerability relied on predictable DNS transaction IDs and predictable UDP source ports (low entropy) in many caching resolvers, making it feasible for attackers to race legitimate responses and inject forged answers into resolver caches (B). DNSSEC validation failures (A) are unrelated to Kaminsky’s technique. IPv6-only resolvers (C) are irrelevant to the fundamental predictor problem. Weak TLS certificate validation (D) pertains to TLS and HTTPS, not to DNS UDP transaction ID / port entropy issues exploited in that era.

question: While performing a network engagement you craft packets with a forged source IP equal to the gateway’s IP so that target hosts send replies to you. This technique—commonly used to intercept traffic indirectly or to facilitate reflection/amplification attacks—is known as:

options.A: IP spoofing
options.B: MAC spoofing
options.C: DNS spoofing
options.D: Email spoofing

explanation: IP spoofing (A) is the deliberate falsification of the IP source address field in an IP packet so that the packet appears to originate from another host (e.g., the gateway). This can be used to induce replies to be sent to the spoofed address (useful in reflection/amplification attacks) or, when combined with other techniques, to facilitate interception. MAC spoofing (B) alters the link-layer source (useful for port stealing/ARP tricks) but does not change the IP header. DNS spoofing (C) is about fabricating DNS responses to redirect names to attacker-controlled addresses, not forging IP headers. Email spoofing (D) forges SMTP headers (From:) to impersonate senders; it’s an application-layer spoof, not the network-layer technique described. In CEHv13 terms IP spoofing is an L3 technique that can support sniffing by enabling traffic redirection or by evading source-based filtering.

question: You query RDAP for example.com and see: "entities":[{"roles":["registrar"]},{"roles":["registrant"],"vcardArray":[... "fn":"Domains By Proxy" ...]}] and "status":["clientTransferProhibited"]. What is the MOST accurate interpretation for footprinting?

options.A: The domain is unlocked for transfer and the real registrant’s full PII is available in RDAP
options.B: The registrant is the same as the registrar and transfer is unrestricted
options.C: The domain uses DNSSEC validation and transfer must occur via EPP auth-info only
options.D: The domain is privacy-shielded (proxy service listed as registrant), and the registrar has set a client-side transfer lock that would need deliberate removal to transfer

explanation: “Domains By Proxy” (or similar) indicates a privacy/proxy service masking the actual registrant; "clientTransferProhibited" reflects an EPP status preventing transfer until unlocked—key signals for ownership and contact escalation paths. A is wrong: the status shows locked and registrant PII is masked. B misreads roles; registrar and registrant are distinct entities. C mentions DNSSEC and EPP specifics not evidenced; RDAP status does not imply DNSSEC, and transfer locks are independent of DNSSEC presence.

question: An attacker on a routed internal segment injects crafted TCP packets with predicted sequence and acknowledgment numbers, sending RST/ACK frames to desynchronize a client–server flow and then inserting spoofed data to assume the client’s identity. What category of session hijacking is this?

options.A: Passive network hijacking
options.B: Session fixation
options.C: Man-in-the-browser (MitB)
options.D: Active TCP session hijacking

explanation: The scenario describes active TCP session hijacking because the attacker manipulates an existing TCP connection by desynchronizing endpoints and injecting spoofed packets with guessed sequence/ACK numbers; classic techniques include blind/non-blind hijacking, RST/FIN desync, and keystroke injection, historically demonstrated with tools like Hunt/Juggernaut and modern packet crafting (Scapy). A is incorrect because passive hijacking limits itself to sniffing/monitoring traffic without modifying it. B is incorrect as fixation pertains to web application session IDs and authentication flows, not transport-layer sequence manipulation. C is incorrect because MitB uses malware to hook the browser/DOM and alter transactions locally, not to inject raw TCP segments on the network.

question: Your blue team suspects low-and-slow C2 using jittered beacons, domain fronting/CDN cover traffic, and rotating TLS client fingerprints. Known IOCs are ineffective. Which IDS detection approach provides the BEST chance of discovery?

options.A: Strict signature matching on known C2 URIs and JA3 hashes from past campaigns
options.B: Detonating downloaded binaries in a sandbox to look for process injections
options.C: Network behavior anomaly detection with baselining (e.g., periodicity drift, DNS request entropy, TLS JA3/JA4 outliers, rare SNI)
options.D: Port-based allowlists that restrict traffic to TCP/443 and TCP/80 only

explanation: Behavior/anomaly analytics identify statistical deviations (beacon periodicity with jitter, rare destinations, DNS entropy changes, TLS fingerprint anomalies) even when adversaries evade static IOCs via fronting and rotation; tools like Zeek plus ML/UEBA can baseline norms and surface outliers. A fails when indicators are intentionally varied. B is valuable for file-based threats but misses pure network beacons that never drop binaries. D is ineffective because modern C2 hides in allowed ports (80/443); port controls alone cannot detect covert channels within legitimate services.

question: During testing, you find that a PHP application connects to MySQL using the account webapp_user with GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* permissions. Which is the MOST critical risk of this misconfiguration?

options.A: Attackers could exploit CSRF tokens to escalate their session privileges
options.B: Exploitation of SQL injection would allow full database control, including schema modification and user management
options.C: Cross-site scripting could leak sensitive cookies to the attacker
options.D: Denial-of-service due to excessive use of LIMIT queries

explanation: Assigning ALL PRIVILEGES to a web application account means that any SQL injection allows total compromise: creating/dropping tables, escalating privileges, creating users, and full data exfiltration (B). CSRF (A) is unrelated to DB permissions. XSS (C) is a separate client-side risk. Excessive use of LIMIT (D) may cause performance issues but is not the critical issue of misconfiguration here. Best practice is least privilege: grant only SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on specific schemas.

question: A staffer receives a LinkedIn connection request from the “CFO” with a profile URL of linkedin.com/in/michaeI-johnson that looks correct at a glance; the account has a professionally written bio, the CFO’s stolen headshot, and dozens of mutual connections the staffer doesn’t actually know personally. Which indicator MOST strongly signals an impersonation using a look-alike account?

options.A: The account has under 200 connections and limited posting history
options.B: The profile URL/handle uses homoglyphs (e.g., uppercase “I” instead of lowercase “l”) to mimic the real name
options.C: The account posts frequently about corporate achievements and charity events
options.D: The account lists a prior employer that the real CFO once worked at

explanation: Homoglyph abuse (B)—such as substituting Latin “l” with uppercase “I” or Cyrillic characters—creates deceptive, look-alike handles and is a high-fidelity signal of impersonation on social platforms; this is a classic account-establishment technique (MITRE ATT&CK: T1585.001 Social Media Accounts) used in executive-impersonation schemes. A small network or young account (A) can be legitimate for some users and is a weak signal by itself. Posting about company initiatives (C) is easily cloned from public PR and does not prove illegitimacy. A prior employer match (D) can be scraped from the real executive’s public résumé; alone it does not confirm a fake.

question: During a web exploitation test, the attacker uses overlapping IP fragments and contradictory TCP segment sequence numbers so that the target OS reconstructs a payload that the NIDS never sees. The pcap on the sensor shows all packets, but no alert triggers and the server is compromised. Which evasion technique is MOST likely in use?

options.A: Polymorphic shellcode to evade byte-pattern signatures
options.B: Target-based reassembly mismatch (fragment/stream overlap) to desynchronize IDS and host
options.C: Alert flooding to bury true positives in noise
options.D: TCP ACK scan to hide open ports in plain sight

explanation: B is correct because overlapping fragments and conflicting TCP sequences exploit differences between an IDS’s normalizer/reassembler and the endpoint TCP/IP stack, causing the IDS to assemble a benign stream while the host reconstructs the malicious bytes; this is classic insertion/evasion per Ptacek–Newsham. A focuses on payload mutation and would not explain the contradictory sequencing/reassembly behavior. C (alert flooding) increases volume but does not account for a missed alert on an observed exploit stream. D (ACK scanning) is a stealth reconnaissance technique and unrelated to differential reassembly of exploit payloads.

question: During a quick TLS check on a newly deployed API endpoint, you want to open a live handshake to print the full certificate chain, negotiated protocol/cipher, and ALPN while correctly sending SNI. Which command is the MOST appropriate?

options.A: nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 api.example.com
options.B: openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -alpn h2,http/1.1 -showcerts
options.C: openssl x509 -in server.crt -text -noout
options.D: keytool -list -keystore server.jks

explanation: openssl s_client performs a real TLS handshake and prints the negotiated protocol/cipher, ALPN, OCSP stapling, and the exact server-sent chain (with -showcerts), and -servername ensures SNI is used, making B correct. A runs an NSE script that enumerates ciphers without necessarily showing the actual chain from a single live connection; it is excellent for breadth but not for the specific “show this handshake’s chain” requirement. C only decodes a local certificate file and provides no handshake details. D lists entries inside a Java keystore, not a remote server’s live TLS negotiation. In CEHv13 tooling, openssl s_client is the standard, quick on-box probe for certificate/handshake verification.

question: A threat actor gained access to a cloud workload and attempts to enumerate secrets by scanning environment variables, mounted volumes, and metadata endpoints. Which combined preventive configuration MOST reduces this reconnaissance success?

options.A: Automount service account tokens disabled by default, restrict hostPath mounts, and use IAM roles with least-privilege (no wildcard permissions)
options.B: Increase pod CPU and memory limits so the attacker cannot list environment variables due to throttling
options.C: Enable detailed application-level debug logging to trace attacker activity
options.D: Allow all service accounts to read metadata for transparency, but enforce encryption-at-rest on secrets

explanation: Correct Answer: A. Disabling automatic service account token mount (automountServiceAccountToken: false), forbidding or strictly controlling hostPath mounts, and enforcing least-privilege IAM roles reduce the avenues an attacker can use to retrieve credentials (no accessible tokens, no host filesystem access) and limit what an attacker can do if they obtain a token. Option B (increasing resource limits) does not prevent secrets discovery and is irrelevant to reconnaissance. Option C (debug logging) may help detection but can leak sensitive info and is reactive rather than preventive. Option D is counterproductive—allowing all service accounts to read metadata increases exposure; encryption-at-rest without access controls or token protections does not block metadata/token theft.

question: A blue team deploys application whitelisting (AppLocker/WDAC) and an EDR tuned to block unknown binaries. The red team still executes payloads by launching trusted, signed Windows utilities (e.g., script hosts and registration tools) that fetch and run attacker-controlled logic without writing a new EXE. Which technique is being used to evade endpoint controls?

options.A: Living-off-the-land via signed binary proxy execution (LOLBins)
options.B: Kernel Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) rootkit persistence
options.C: BIOS/UEFI firmware reflashing for pre-boot persistence
options.D: User Account Control (UAC) bypass through consent UI spoofing alone

explanation: Using signed, native binaries (LOLBins) such as regsvr32, mshta, rundll32, or installutil to proxy malicious content is a well-known defense-evasion method (MITRE ATT&CK T1218) that slips past basic whitelisting and some signature checks because the launcher is trusted; robust policy must explicitly constrain these binaries’ behaviors (e.g., WDAC deny rules, Constrained Language Mode, child-process, and network egress controls). B and C are advanced persistence vectors but do not match the observed reliance on trusted user-mode binaries to execute payloads. D may elevate privileges in some cases but does not inherently explain execution under strict whitelisting without new binaries.

question: Which Windows mechanism allows an attacker to store data in a file system location that is not shown by ordinary directory listings (e.g., dir or Explorer), and is commonly abused to hide small files or payloads without creating visible files?

options.A: NTFS Alternate Data Streams (ADS)
options.B: FAT32 hidden attribute bit
options.C: BitLocker encrypted container
options.D: NTFS compression via Compact attribute

explanation: Option A is correct because NTFS Alternate Data Streams (ADS) provide additional named streams attached to a file (or directory) that are not visible in normal directory listings and are not separate filesystem entries; attackers can hide small payloads, configuration data, or shellcode in ADS and the data will often be invisible to casual inspection. CEH covers ADS as a stealthy storage technique and defenders search for streams (forensic tools and PowerShell modules can enumerate them). Option B is incorrect because FAT32’s “hidden” attribute is a visible filesystem metadata flag that Explorer and dir will respect (hidden files can be revealed by changing view settings), whereas ADS are not separate directory entries. Option C (BitLocker) is encryption-at-rest for volumes; it protects confidentiality but is not a hiding mechanism for covert storage within an existing file system namespace. Option D (NTFS compression) simply compresses the primary data stream to save space; it does not create a hidden secondary stream and is not intended or typically used to conceal separate payloads. Defensive controls include scanning for ADS, enabling file-integrity monitoring, and restricting write access to high-risk locations.

question: A camera vendor’s OTA process was abused to push altered firmware to a historian-adjacent appliance. What countermeasure most robustly protects the firmware supply chain end-to-end?

options.A: Signed firmware with an immutable root-of-trust (secure boot) verified by the bootloader before install, using offline-protected signing keys, version rollback protection, and staged/canary rollout controls
options.B: Hosting updates on HTTPS with a valid public CA certificate
options.C: Packing binaries with UPX to deter reverse engineering
options.D: Hashing the file on the update server and publishing the hash on the vendor blog

explanation: Only a device-enforced chain of trust (secure boot + signature verification using keys outside the update server’s control), plus rollback protection and staged deployment, resists server compromise and MITM; it ensures only vendor-authorized images are accepted. B (HTTPS) secures transport but not the image if the server is compromised. C (obfuscation) is not a security boundary. D (published hashes) can be spoofed alongside a compromised server and is not verified by the device, so it lacks enforceability.

question: Which sequence most accurately represents a standard, defensible SQL injection testing methodology from reconnaissance through reporting?

options.A: Exploit -> Escalate -> Discover -> Report -> Clean up
options.B: Discover injection points -> Fingerprint DBMS -> Validate via controlled probes -> Safely extract data (if authorized) -> Document evidence and remediation -> Clean up/restore
options.C: Run a full automated scan -> Exploit every positive finding -> Erase all logs to hide activity -> Report findings without reproduction steps
options.D: Random fuzzing of all inputs -> Immediate UNION extraction -> Publish findings on public channels to pressure the client

explanation: Option B describes the correct, defensible workflow: first discover injection points, then fingerprint the DBMS, validate using controlled, non-destructive probes, extract data only if in scope and authorized (with caution), thoroughly document evidence and remediation steps, and clean up or restore any changed state. This flow aligns with CEH best practices and professional engagement rules. Option A is unordered and irresponsible (exploitation before discovery is illogical). Option C is unethical and dangerous (erasing logs and indiscriminately exploiting). Option D is chaotic, unprofessional, and could lead to legal/contractual violations; responsible methodology avoids random destructive actions and public disclosure.

question: A financial services company wants to prevent malware from exploiting unpatched browsers and plug-ins. Which defense is MOST aligned with CEH malware countermeasures?

options.A: Implementing application whitelisting and auto-patching software updates
options.B: Disabling TLS 1.2 to force clients to use TLS 1.3 only
options.C: Creating a DNS blacklist of all non–.com domains
options.D: Instructing employees to avoid browsing social media websites

explanation: A is correct because malware often exploits outdated software; auto-patching reduces exploitable vulnerabilities, and application whitelisting ensures only trusted binaries run. B (TLS 1.2 disabling) doesn’t address malware exploits. C (non-.com blocklists) is arbitrary and easily bypassed. D (user instruction alone) is insufficient; attackers exploit trusted sites and drive-by downloads. CEH stresses layered defense: patching, whitelisting, sandboxing, and hardening browsers.

question: You have brief, legitimate physical access to an unlocked Android device where Developer Options are enabled. The target app’s manifest shows android:allowBackup="true" and no custom backup rules. Which technique most directly enables extraction of the app’s data for analysis?

options.A: Trigger BLE pairing with the app’s wearable companion and pull data from GATT characteristics
options.B: Use logical backup mechanisms (e.g., ADB/Auto Backup) to obtain the app’s private files and databases
options.C: Attempt kernel privilege escalation to dump /data using an n-day exploit
options.D: Perform Wi-Fi deauthentication to capture WPA2 handshakes for later decryption of app traffic

explanation: With allowBackup=true, Android’s backup transports (including ADB in appropriate contexts or Auto Backup to eligible storage) can include app-private data unless excluded/encrypted by policy—so B is correct. BLE pairing (A) concerns radio peripherals and won’t access private app storage. Kernel exploitation (C) is unnecessary, high risk, and out of scope when backup is allowed. Wi-Fi deauth (D) targets network credentials/handshakes, not on-device app data.

question: A privileged dashboard is fronted by a CDN. Responses include Cache-Control: public, max-age=900 with no Vary on Cookie or Authorization. After an admin views the page, some unauthenticated users intermittently receive the admin-rendered dashboard from the CDN. What vulnerability BEST fits this behavior?

options.A: CSRF due to sensitive actions accessible via GET
options.B: Insecure CORS allowing credentialed cross-origin reads
options.C: Missing HSTS permitting downgrade attacks
options.D: Authorization-unaware caching (cache key lacks user/auth context), leading to cache poisoning/leakage

explanation: Marking authenticated, user-specific content as public and omitting Vary on identity signals lets a shared cache serve privileged content to other users—an authorization failure at the caching layer (D). CSRF (A) is about forging requests, not serving someone else’s cached response. CORS (B) is unrelated: the CDN leaks to any requester regardless of origin. HSTS (C) ensures HTTPS but does not prevent serving cached admin content to others. Fix by using Cache-Control: private, no-store for personalized pages or segmenting cache keys by Authorization/Cookie/surrogate key and validating headers at the edge.

question: During mutual TLS testing, the client’s certificate is accepted by the server’s CA chain, but authentication consistently fails. On inspection, the certificate lacks the Client Authentication OID in the Extended Key Usage field. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: The certificate was signed with RSA instead of ECC
options.B: The certificate does not include a Subject Key Identifier
options.C: The certificate is missing the correct Extended Key Usage for client authentication
options.D: The certificate chain uses SHA-1 instead of SHA-256

explanation: In mTLS, the client’s certificate must include Extended Key Usage (EKU) with Client Authentication OID (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.2). Without this, the server rejects it even if it is signed by a trusted CA, making C correct. A is wrong because RSA vs ECC does not affect authentication validity if supported. B is incorrect—Subject Key Identifier helps with path building but isn’t mandatory for client auth. D is wrong because SHA-1 affects trustworthiness but does not directly block EKU-based client auth. CEHv13 stresses knowledge of EKU fields for proper certificate functionality.

question: An attacker is push-bombing engineers with dozens of MFA approvals at 02:00, eventually coercing a tired user to tap “Approve.” Which control is the MOST effective technical countermeasure against this class of social engineering?

options.A: Require SMS OTP as the primary factor for all users
options.B: Increase security-awareness frequency from annual to quarterly
options.C: Lock accounts for 60 minutes after five denied push prompts
options.D: Replace push approvals with phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn authenticators and enable number-matching / rate-limiting for any residual push flows

explanation: D directly neutralizes consent-coercion by eliminating phishable/push-based approvals in favor of origin-bound FIDO2/WebAuthn, while adding number-matching and rate limits where push persists; this addresses both the human and protocol vectors and is current best practice. A (SMS) is vulnerable to SIM-swap/SS7 issues and does not stop fatigue attacks initiated through push. B improves awareness but is insufficient against engineered UI spam. C reduces some noise but remains susceptible to carefully timed or distributed prompts and does not remove the root phishability of push.

question: While testing a single-page application (SPA), you find that sensitive data such as API keys and user tokens are stored in localStorage. Why is this a client-side security concern?

options.A: localStorage is encrypted by the browser and safe from all attackers
options.B: Any script running in the browser context, including injected malicious JavaScript from an XSS attack, can access localStorage values
options.C: localStorage enforces SameSite rules, making CSRF impossible
options.D: Values in localStorage are automatically protected by TLS

explanation: Storing sensitive values in localStorage is dangerous because they are accessible to any JavaScript executing in the page context, including malicious scripts injected via XSS (B). Option A is false: there is no encryption at rest in the browser. Option C is misleading: SameSite affects cookies, not localStorage. Option D is irrelevant because TLS protects in transit but not storage within the client. Best practice is to store session tokens in Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite cookies.

question: A red team must validate a stateless edge filter’s resilience to custom TCP probes that vary flags (e.g., NULL/Xmas/FIN), spoof sources, tweak TTL/offsets, and optionally fragment to bypass naive port/flag rules. They want a command-line packet crafter that can generate arbitrary TCP/UDP/ICMP frames and measure responses in real time. Which tool BEST fits?

options.A: Burp Suite
options.B: sqlmap
options.C: Hydra
options.D: hping3

explanation: hping3 is a flexible packet crafting utility allowing arbitrary flag sets, source address spoofing, TTL/ID control, fragmentation, and timing, with built-in response analysis—ideal for firewall evasion and measurement of stateless filter behavior. A (Burp Suite) focuses on HTTP/S proxying and app-layer testing, not raw packet crafting. B (sqlmap) targets SQL injection and is unrelated to L3/L4 evasion. C (Hydra) is for password guessing over known services, not generating custom frames to probe firewall behaviors.

question: An organization configures MDM policies to prevent jailbroken devices from accessing corporate resources. A user bypasses this by installing a jailbreak detection evasion tool that hides modifications from MDM checks. What weakness is this scenario highlighting?

options.A: Reliance on client-side only jailbreak detection without server-side validation
options.B: Overuse of mobile app wrapping for encryption
options.C: Forcing TLS 1.3 only in corporate VPN tunnels
options.D: Disabling biometric authentication in favor of passcodes

explanation: Client-side jailbreak detection can be bypassed by evasion tools; robust MDM must integrate server-side validation and attestation (A). App wrapping (B) is a protective measure but unrelated. TLS enforcement (C) addresses secure transport, not jailbreak checks. Biometric settings (D) affect authentication strength, not jailbreak detection.

question: You are testing an enterprise NFS deployment. rpcbind (TCP/111) responds and UDP/TCP 2049 are reachable. You need to enumerate export paths and client restrictions before attempting any mounts. Which single action MOST directly achieves this?

options.A: Run nmap --script nfs-ls -p 2049 <target> to list files in exported directories
options.B: Query rpcbind with rpcinfo -p <target> and assume any nfs/mountd program numbers equal mountable exports
options.C: Perform a SYN scan on all high ports to find mountd and infer exports from open ports
options.D: Use showmount -e <target> to request the export list (paths and access controls) from mountd

explanation: showmount -e queries the mountd service to return the export list (paths and client/netgroup restrictions) and is the canonical first step for NFS enumeration (D). nfs-ls (A) attempts directory listing of already mounted exports and presumes you can mount or that NFSv4 is configured to expose a pseudo-root; it’s not the discovery step. rpcinfo -p (B) only shows registered RPC programs and versions, not the export table. A high-port SYN scan (C) may locate mountd’s dynamic port, but it won’t disclose which directories are exported or their access controls.

question: A program manager asks for a quarterly cycle that begins with discovery scans, proceeds to validated credentialed scans, and ends with selected manual verification of critical web findings before reporting. Which classification BEST describes this end-to-end methodology?

options.A: External black-box penetration test with exploit development focus
options.B: Continuous monitoring only, using passive sensors and threat intel feeds
options.C: Layered vulnerability assessment program combining unauthenticated discovery, authenticated host assessment, and targeted manual application validation (DAST)
options.D: Single-phase compliance audit aligned solely to CIS benchmarks

explanation: D is incorrect because an exploit-centric pen test is goal-oriented and not the described cyclical assessment flow. B is incorrect because the workflow includes active scanning and manual validation, not passive-only monitoring. D is incorrect again because a single-phase benchmark audit omits discovery scans and manual application validation. C is correct as it accurately reflects a layered vulnerability assessment program typical in CEHv13 practice: initial unauthenticated discovery (e.g., Nmap/host discovery), followed by authenticated host scanning (e.g., Nessus/Qualys/OpenVAS with credentials) for accurate patch/config state, and selective manual DAST validation of web findings (e.g., Burp/ZAP) to reduce false positives before formal reporting.

question: Your organization wants to degrade the fidelity of large-scale UDP service discovery on Internet-facing ranges without breaking production apps. Which network control MOST directly reduces the effectiveness of mass UDP scans?

options.A: Enable PMTU black-hole detection on routers.
options.B: Configure hosts and firewalls to silently drop (or heavily rate-limit) ICMP Destination Unreachable—Port Unreachable (Type 3, Code 3) for closed UDP ports.
options.C: Block ICMP Echo Requests globally.
options.D: Disable TCP window scaling on edge servers.

explanation: UDP scanning typically classifies a port as “closed” only upon receiving ICMP Type 3 Code 3. By dropping or throttling these messages, defenders force scanners to see silence, yielding “open|filtered” and greatly reducing the attacker’s ability to map UDP exposure; this must be balanced against troubleshooting needs since suppressing ICMP can hinder diagnostics. PMTU features (A) don’t affect UDP port state classification. ICMP Echo filtering (C) pertains to ping sweeps, not UDP port discovery. TCP window scaling (D) has no bearing on UDP.

question: The client wants an external test that realistically simulates an internet-based adversary with no internal knowledge or credentials. Which testing approach best fits this requirement?

options.A: White-box testing
options.B: Crystal-box testing with developer interviews
options.C: Gray-box testing with limited credentials and diagrams
options.D: Black-box testing

explanation: Black-box testing simulates an attacker with no prior internal knowledge (no creds, code, or architecture docs); therefore D is correct. A/B (white/crystal-box) provide full internal visibility (source, configs), which contradicts the requirement. C (gray-box) grants partial knowledge (e.g., limited creds, network maps) and does not fully model an uninformed external adversary. CEH uses these model distinctions to align test realism with objectives and constraints.

question: You discover TCP/445 open on a Windows server while TCP/139 and UDP/137/138 are closed (NetBIOS over TCP/IP disabled). You need domain and share reconnaissance with minimal privileges. Which approach is MOST effective?

options.A: nbtstat -A <IP> to retrieve the NetBIOS name table for users and shares
options.B: net view <IP> /all using the current workstation context to list everything
options.C: enum4linux -a <IP> to drive SMB/RPC (e.g., SAMR/LSARPC/SRVSVC) enumeration over 445 with null/guest where possible
options.D: Launch LLMNR spoofing (Responder) to coerce credentials and infer shares from captured hashes

explanation: With NetBIOS disabled, NBNS/NBTSTAT (A) won’t work; SMB still runs natively over 445, and enum4linux aggregates numerous RPC calls (SRVSVC for shares, SAMR for users/groups, LSARPC for policies) to enumerate rich data even with null/guest access (C). net view (B) may require valid credentials and often returns limited data. LLMNR spoofing (D) is an active credential-coercion attack, not direct enumeration of the target’s shares or domain info; it also risks detection and is outside “enumeration via service” scope.

question: A web application is protected by a simple WAF that blocks common SQL metacharacters and known attack signatures. During testing you find that sending UN/**/ION/**/SELEC/**/T allows a UNION payload to succeed while UNION SELECT is blocked. Which evasion technique does this demonstrate?

options.A: Inline comment obfuscation (inserting comments inside keywords)
options.B: Base64-encoding the entire payload and relying on the server to decode it
options.C: Using stacked queries to append another statement after the original
options.D: Forcing the DBMS to use OOB DNS callbacks for exfiltration

explanation: Correct — Option A (inline comment obfuscation) inserts SQL comments (e.g., /**/) or other benign tokens inside SQL keywords to break simple signature-based WAF pattern matching while leaving the DBMS parser able to reassemble the keyword (UN/**/ION -> UNION). This is a classic evasion technique often used alongside other obfuscations (case-mixing, whitespace substitution). Option B (base64-encoding) would only work if the application decodes input server-side before SQL execution; this is uncommon for typical form parameters and is not what the example shows. Option C (stacked queries) is a different technique that executes multiple statements via statement delimiters (e.g., ;) and does not explain why inserting inline comments inside keywords would succeed. Option D (OOB DNS callbacks) is an exfiltration channel, not an evasion of keyword-based WAF signatures. In CEHv13 practice, inline-comment obfuscation is an explicit evasion taught for bypassing naïve pattern-based defenses.

question: During passive profiling, you collect robots.txt and sitemap.xml from the primary domain. What is the MOST accurate way these artifacts should influence your web infrastructure footprinting?

options.A: Use them to derive candidate paths and endpoints (including disallowed admin/debug routes), then corroborate with archival sources (Wayback Machine, URL indexes) and cautiously probe with HEAD/GET; they are reconnaissance inputs, not vulnerabilities by themselves
options.B: Treat any Disallow entry as proof of a critical access control flaw and report immediately
options.C: Ignore robots.txt because compliant crawlers never index sensitive paths and attackers can’t access them
options.D: Use sitemap URLs only for SEO context; they have no value in security testing

explanation: robots.txt and sitemap.xml often expose otherwise unlinked endpoints and historical routes; in footprinting, you mine these files to seed endpoint lists and then validate safely (e.g., HEAD, low-rate GET), potentially discovering admin panels, feature flags, or legacy APIs. They are not vulnerabilities on their own—access controls must still be tested. Declaring every Disallow a flaw (B) is incorrect. Ignoring robots (C) misunderstands that attackers do not honor crawler conventions. Dismissing sitemaps (D) wastes a rich source of structured URLs that often include versioned or language-specific paths useful for breadth coverage.

question: You capture the following NBSTAT snippet for a domain member: “ACME GROUP” “ACME GROUP” “ACME UNIQUE” “WS-ENG-12 UNIQUE” Which entry BEST indicates the list of all domain controllers registered for the domain?

options.A: ACME <1B> UNIQUE
options.B: ACME <1D> UNIQUE
options.C: ACME <1C> GROUP
options.D: ACME <00> GROUP

explanation: The GROUP name is registered by all domain controllers in the domain and is used to locate DCs for services like logon and LDAP/Kerberos referral (C); this is the most reliable NBSTAT indicator of DC presence as a set. UNIQUE (A) is the Domain Master Browser, typically the PDC Emulator—one system, not all DCs. UNIQUE (B) would represent a local Master Browser on a subnet (not shown here and unrelated to DCs). GROUP (D) is the workgroup/domain name for browser service purposes, not specific to DCs and generally registered by many systems, making it a poor DC enumerator.

question: A security team is standardizing their IPsec ESP configurations and wants a single cipher suite that provides confidentiality and integrity in one primitive and is widely supported by modern stacks. Which option is the BEST choice?

options.A: AES-256-CBC for encryption and HMAC-MD5 for integrity
options.B: 3DES-EDE-CBC with HMAC-SHA1 for backward compatibility
options.C: AES-128-GCM (AEAD) for ESP
options.D: RC4-HMAC for ESP to reduce CPU cost

explanation: AES-GCM is an AEAD mode standardized for IPsec ESP that provides authenticated encryption in one construction, reduces complexity (no separate MAC to configure), and is widely supported in modern VPN implementations, making C correct. A combines CBC (which lacks built-in integrity) with a weak HMAC choice (MD5) and is not recommended. B relies on 3DES and SHA-1—both legacy and discouraged due to performance and security concerns (e.g., SWEET32 and SHA-1 deprecation). D is incorrect because RC4 is not appropriate for IPsec ESP and is widely deprecated due to significant cryptographic weaknesses.

question: An engineering team built an internal service using AES-GCM but implemented a device-scoped 96-bit nonce that is randomly generated once and then reused for every message from that device. What countermeasure MOST directly prevents catastrophic GCM nonce-reuse failures?

options.A: Keep the single random nonce but upgrade the key to AES-256-GCM
options.B: Generate a unique per-message 96-bit nonce (e.g., an atomic counter combined with a device-unique prefix), enforce rekeying before counter wraparound, and use a vetted library that guarantees nonce uniqueness
options.C: Switch to AES-CBC with a zero IV to eliminate nonce requirements
options.D: Append a SHA-256 checksum to the ciphertext to detect reuse

explanation: AES-GCM requires a unique nonce per key; reuse breaks both confidentiality and integrity. The fix is to guarantee per-message nonce uniqueness (counter-based or secure RNG), rekey before wrap, and rely on vetted libraries that enforce this invariant; thus B is correct. A (AES-256) does not mitigate nonce reuse. C replaces one serious flaw with another (CBC with static IV is insecure and still needs authentication). D adds a non-keyed checksum that does not prevent or detect GCM-forgery conditions.

question: A CISO requests that the “Executive Summary” of your vulnerability assessment report be decision-ready for the board. Which content set BEST satisfies this requirement without overwhelming non-technical stakeholders?

options.A: Full scan logs, raw plugin output, and packet captures demonstrating each exploit attempt.
options.B: A detailed CVSS vector breakdown for every finding, including temporal/environmental metrics per asset.
options.C: A concise risk narrative with business impact highlights, top 5 risks with trend (last 3 quarters), risk heat map, MTTR by severity, and high-level remediation plan/SLA owners.
options.D: A comprehensive list of all hosts and open ports discovered, grouped by subnet and service.

explanation: C is correct because Executive Summaries in CEHv13-aligned reports translate technical findings into business risk, showing risk concentration and trajectory (trend), key KPIs (e.g., Mean Time to Remediate per severity), and clear accountability (owners/SLAs) with visuals like heat maps; this informs resource decisions without technical noise. A is incorrect because full logs/pcaps belong in technical appendices, not the executive section. B is incorrect since detailed CVSS vectors for every item overwhelm non-technical readers and are better placed in technical sections or annexes. D is incorrect because host/port inventories are discovery artifacts; while useful to engineers, they do not directly communicate risk/business impact at the leadership level.

question: You’re creating detections for a packed info-stealer whose on-disk variants change constantly. Sandbox shows that after unpacking, the payload consistently creates a mutex “GlobalK2Sync” and emits a family-specific config header in memory. Which approach provides the MOST resilient anti-malware detection?

options.A: Hashing the full file and adding the SHA-256 to blocklists across the fleet
options.B: Flagging any executable compiled with a common packer such as UPX or MPRESS
options.C: YARA rules that target stable post-unpack artifacts (mutex string, config header bytes, protocol markers) and memory scanning of live processes via the AV/EDR engine
options.D: Alerting on any process that opens \Device\PhysicalMemory during execution

explanation: C is correct because rules built from stable, family-unique post-unpack indicators and applied to memory/dumped images are packer-agnostic and robust; many engines support memory scanning and “post-unpack” hooks. A fails on trivial repacks. B is noisy and blocks benign packed software. D is obsolete on modern Windows and non-specific to this family. CEH malware analysis/countermeasure guidance stresses dynamic-aided static detection (YARA), memory inspection, and focusing on family-unique toolmarks.

question: A 700-Gbps CLDAP/DNS reflection saturates the link to your data center. Servers and WAFs are healthy but unreachable due to bandwidth exhaustion. What is the MOST effective immediate action to restore availability to critical services?

options.A: Scale out the web tier and increase auto-scaling thresholds
options.B: Add stricter WAF rules and CAPTCHAs on login endpoints
options.C: Tune Linux network stacks (e.g., net.core.somaxconn) to increase queue depths
options.D: Divert traffic through a cloud scrubbing provider via BGP redirect/GRE tunnels (or provider anycast scrubbing)

explanation: Volumetric reflection attacks overwhelm the circuit before traffic reaches your stack; traffic diversion to a cloud scrubbing service (BGP-based redirection to anycast scrubbing centers with GRE/IPsec return of clean traffic) is the correct immediate response, often coordinated with your ISP. Option A doesn’t help when the link is saturated. Option B is Layer-7 and irrelevant when packets can’t reach your WAF. Option C improves server queues but cannot fix upstream bandwidth exhaustion; the choke point is the circuit, not the host.

question: For application-level interception, modifying HTTP requests/responses, and session token manipulation while testing web apps (including automated replay and scripting), which tool is the industry standard proxy?

options.A: ZAP (OWASP Zed Attack Proxy)
options.B: mitmproxy
options.C: Burp Suite
options.D: Nikto

explanation: Burp Suite is the industry standard interception proxy used by web application testers to intercept, inspect, modify, and replay HTTP/HTTPS requests and responses, tamper with cookies/session tokens, run automated scanners, and chain modules (Intruder, Repeater, Sequencer) for session-related analysis — it’s the canonical application-level tool in CEH/OWASP testing. ZAP (A) is a capable open-source proxy with many of the same features and is widely used (especially for automation), but Burp is often regarded as the more feature-rich, commercial standard in professional web app testing. mitmproxy (B) is a scriptable, lightweight interception proxy that is excellent for automated and programmable MITM tasks (and may be preferred for scripting), but Burp provides a more complete suite of web security testing modules and a GUI geared to manual app-level session analysis. Nikto (D) is a web server scanner that finds misconfigurations and known issues — it does not provide interactive request/response interception or token manipulation.

question: A staffing agency places temporary personnel in your call center for peak season. To minimize insider-threat risk while sustaining productivity, which control set is BEST?

options.A: NDA agreements, annual awareness training, and generic VPN accounts shared among temps
options.B: Just-in-time (JIT) privileged access via PAM with time-boxed approvals, strict segregation of duties, and least privilege role profiles for temps
options.C: Outbound web proxy with SSL inspection and verbose logging only
options.D: File integrity monitoring on production servers without changes to access provisioning

explanation: Insider risk is reduced by granting only the minimum necessary entitlements and only when needed: JIT via PAM prevents standing privileges; time-boxed approvals, SoD, and least-privilege role profiles limit misuse scope and duration; NDAs and training (A) are necessary but insufficient and shared accounts eliminate accountability; outbound proxy/logging (C) aids detection but not prevention or scope limitation; file integrity monitoring (D) detects server changes but does nothing to prevent inappropriate access grants or data viewing by temps.

question: An attacker sets up a fake captive portal that mimics a legitimate Wi-Fi login page, tricking users into entering their corporate credentials. What type of wireless threat is this?

options.A: Evil Twin with phishing portal
options.B: Dictionary attack
options.C: Bluejacking
options.D: Initialization vector collision

explanation: An Evil Twin with a phishing portal tricks users into connecting to a rogue AP and submitting credentials through a fake web interface; A is correct. B is incorrect because dictionary attacks target captured handshakes offline. C is incorrect since bluejacking relates to sending unsolicited Bluetooth messages, not Wi-Fi. D is incorrect because IV collisions are associated with WEP cracking, not credential phishing portals.

question: A security team detects widespread ARP spoofing alerts affecting multiple VLANs. As a defender, which switch-side control most directly mitigates this sniffing vector by validating ARP packets against trusted bindings at Layer 2?

options.A: MACSec (802.1AE) with AES-GCM on trunk links
options.B: 802.1X EAP-TLS with per-port authentication
options.C: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) with DHCP snooping-built bindings
options.D: IP Source Guard with source IP/MAC filtering on routed interfaces

explanation: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) (C) inspects ARP packets on untrusted ports and validates sender IP/MAC pairs against the DHCP snooping binding table (or static entries), actively blocking ARP spoofing used for sniffing/MITM. MACSec (A) encrypts link-layer traffic between nodes (e.g., on trunks) but does not inspect or block forged ARP on access ports. 802.1X (B) authenticates endpoints but does not validate ARP content once a device is on the network. IP Source Guard (D) enforces source integrity for IPv4/IPv6 but focuses on IP address spoofing at Layer 3 and does not specifically validate ARP opcodes/contents like DAI does.

question: You need to dynamically analyze a suspicious PE that appears to require outbound HTTP(S) before it will unpack and beacon. Your goal is to observe C2 behavior and extract IOCs without risking egress to the Internet. Which lab setup is MOST appropriate?

options.A: A VM bridged to the corporate LAN with only an IDS sensor to watch traffic
options.B: An isolated VM on a host-only/closed network using FakeNet-NG/INetSim to emulate common services, with full packet capture enabled
options.C: A VM using NAT with a firewall rule allowing outbound TCP/80 and TCP/443 for “realistic” C2 observation
options.D: A bare-metal workstation with Wireshark and system restore enabled

explanation: B is correct because host-only isolation plus protocol emulation (FakeNet-NG/INetSim) lets you coerce the sample to reveal DNS/HTTP(S)/SMTP behaviors and endpoints while preventing true egress, yielding safe network and process telemetry for IOC extraction (PCAP, logs). A is unsafe: bridging to production risks lateral movement/data loss even if passively monitored. C intentionally permits egress; while “realistic,” it violates safe analysis practice and can exfiltrate data or stage second-level payloads. D lacks containment, snapshots, and controlled service emulation; a bare-metal host expands risk and impedes repeatable detonation. CEH emphasizes safe dynamic analysis: isolation, snapshots, controlled “Internet,” and layered monitoring (Procmon/Sysmon/PCAP).

question: The blue team observes an abnormal burst of MFA push prompts sent to a single engineer’s device at 02:15, followed by a successful VPN login after one prompt was approved; the engineer later reported being “too tired to keep denying.” From a social-engineering standpoint, what tactic was used?

options.A: Shoulder surfing during a late commute
options.B: MFA fatigue (push bombing) to coerce approval through alert overload
options.C: In-person pretexting to gain workstation access
options.D: Smishing that delivered a malicious APK to the phone

explanation: MFA fatigue attacks bombard users with push notifications until they approve one out of annoyance or confusion, exploiting cognitive overload and poor prompt hygiene; mitigations include number-matching, rate limits, and phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2/WebAuthn). Shoulder surfing (A) involves visually capturing secrets; on-site pretexting (C) would occur physically; smishing (D) uses SMS as a delivery vector and is not necessary for push-spam coercion.

question: During a security review of a microservice, you discover the container has a bind-mount of /var/run/docker.sock from the host and can run docker CLI inside the container. What is the PRIMARY risk introduced by this configuration?

options.A: The container can control the host’s Docker daemon and spawn privileged containers to gain host-level access
options.B: The container can only list local images; it cannot affect the host runtime without --privileged
options.C: The container’s CPU usage will bypass cgroup limits and cause a host DoS condition
options.D: The container image can no longer be scanned accurately by tools like Trivy or Clair

explanation: Mounting the Docker socket gives code inside the container direct API access to the host’s Docker daemon, allowing the attacker to create privileged containers, mount arbitrary host paths, or attach to other containers—effectively escalating to host control; this is a well-known breakout vector documented by red-team playbooks and tools (e.g., using docker run --privileged, mounting /, or leveraging --pid=host). B is incorrect because access to the Docker API enables far more than listing images—privileged containers and host mounts are possible even without the current container itself being --privileged. C is incorrect since cgroup limits still apply to the current container; while a DoS is possible, the socket mount is primarily about privilege escalation, not resource leakage. D is incorrect because scanning accuracy is unrelated to the socket mount; scanners (Trivy/Clair/Anchore) analyze layers/OS packages, not Docker daemon exposure. Defense-in-depth: avoid mounting /var/run/docker.sock, prefer rootless container runtimes, and use admission controls (OPA Gatekeeper/Kyverno) to block such mounts.

question: Your iOS app completes OAuth in a browser and returns to the app using a custom scheme mybank://oauth/callback. A malicious app registers the same scheme first and steals the authorization code. Which control most effectively prevents this interception?

options.A: Enabling CarPlay background modes to isolate network stacks
options.B: Implementing Associated Domains (Universal Links) for the redirect URI and using PKCE with an HTTPS host you control
options.C: Relying on ATS alone to force TLS 1.3 for the redirect
options.D: Enabling Background App Refresh to handle tokens only when the app is foregrounded

explanation: Custom URL schemes are not namespaced and can be hijacked; the robust mitigation is to use Universal Links (Associated Domains) so the redirect targets an HTTPS domain you control that is cryptographically bound to your app, combined with OAuth best practices like PKCE and state validation (B). ATS (C) ensures transport security but cannot prevent handler hijacking. CarPlay modes (A) are irrelevant to redirect routing. Background App Refresh (D) is unrelated to secure redirect owner verification.

question: An attacker on a local network runs a tool that listens for outbound DNS queries and replies with forged DNS answers so clients resolve bank.example.com to an attacker-controlled IP. This is an example of:

options.A: DNS cache poisoning (local/poisoned response injection)
options.B: DNSSEC key compromise
options.C: Zone transfer abuse (AXFR)
options.D: DNS amplification reflection

explanation: This scenario describes DNS cache poisoning (A) where an attacker injects forged DNS responses into a resolver’s cache (or directly answers client queries on the local segment), causing subsequent name lookups to return attacker-controlled IPs (pharming). DNSSEC key compromise (B) would involve stealing or misusing DNS signing keys—an entirely different, higher-privilege event. Zone transfer abuse (C, AXFR) retrieves full DNS zone data from an authoritative server (if misconfigured) but doesn’t itself inject forged responses to make clients resolve names to attacker IPs. DNS amplification/reflection (D) is a volumetric DDoS technique abused to flood victims, not a targeted name-resolution manipulation technique.

question: After compromising a Microsoft 365 Global Administrator, you want durable, low-friction access to mail and files without reusing the user’s password or maintaining a session on their workstation. Which technique provides the MOST stealthy long-term persistence?

options.A: Create Exchange mailbox forwarding rules to an external domain for all users
options.B: Register a multi-tenant Azure AD application and grant Graph application permissions (e.g., Mail.Read, Files.Read.All) via admin consent
options.C: Enable legacy IMAP/POP for the tenant and harvest passwords via brute force
options.D: Add transport rules that bypass spam filtering for attacker IP ranges

explanation: An Azure AD app with admin-consented application permissions uses its own service principal to request Graph access tokens and can read data across the tenant without interactive user logins, providing durable and stealthy persistence (token-based, long-lived secrets/certs); many defenders miss consent governance, making this vector powerful. A is noisy and typically scoped per-mailbox; it also generates user-visible side effects and alertable events. C relies on credentials and weak protocols, is noisy, and often blocked by conditional access. D manipulates hygiene but doesn’t grant durable data access. Defenses: strict OAuth consent governance, app allow-listing, conditional access for service principals, and continuous review of enterprise apps and their grants.

question: A remote site filters most ICMP, and you suspect SNMPv2c is enabled on several routers. You want to identify live SNMP services and extract basic identifiers without brute-forcing communities. Which technique is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Run nmap -sU -p161 -sV --script snmp-info <targets> to identify UDP/161 and gather system details.
options.B: Run nmap -sS -p161 -sV <targets> because SNMP discovery requires TCP SYN on 161/TCP.
options.C: Run ping -s 0 <targets> to bypass ICMP filtering and infer SNMP based on responses.
options.D: Run nbtscan <targets> to enumerate SNMP OIDs over NetBIOS name service.

explanation: SNMP primarily uses UDP/161; nmap -sU -p161 -sV --script snmp-info safely confirms service presence and extracts non-sensitive metadata (e.g., sysDescr, sysName when allowed) without credential attacks, which is aligned with CEHv13 port/service discovery. Option B is incorrect because TCP/161 is uncommon and a SYN scan won’t verify UDP/161. Option C does nothing to reveal SNMP; ICMP behavior does not correlate to UDP/161 service presence. Option D targets NetBIOS Name Service (UDP/137) and cannot enumerate SNMP OIDs; it’s the wrong protocol family.

question: A mail gateway has VRFY and EXPN disabled and tarpits rapid connections, but you still need to enumerate valid internal mailboxes with minimal noise. Which approach remains MOST viable?

options.A: Use POP3 STAT on TCP/110 to list all accounts anonymously
options.B: Conduct RCPT TO probing during an SMTP transaction and analyze 250/550 responses for individual addresses
options.C: Query the gateway’s SPF TXT records to derive internal mailbox names
options.D: Perform IMAP NOOP loops on TCP/143 to extract authenticated user lists from server greetings

explanation: Even when VRFY/EXPN are disabled, many MTAs still reveal acceptance or rejection of recipients during the SMTP envelope phase; carefully throttled RCPT TO probing allows mailbox enumeration by interpreting 250 (accepted) vs 550 (user unknown) responses (B). POP3 STAT (A) and IMAP NOOP (D) require authentication and do not disclose global user lists. SPF TXT records (C) describe sending policy (authorized hosts/MECHs) and provide no directory of mailbox identities; using DNS TXT for enumeration is ineffective. Proper CEH practice includes rate limiting, randomized ordering, and error-handling to avoid detection.

question: Your organization is rolling out IPv6. To prevent rogue IPv6 DHCP servers that hand out attacker-controlled DNS and routes for sniffing/redirects, which Layer-2 control is MOST appropriate?

options.A: DHCPv6 Guard on access ports, permitting DHCPv6 server messages only from trusted interfaces
options.B: RA Guard, allowing only authorized Router Advertisements
options.C: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) across all IPv6 VLANs
options.D: IP Source Guard with static IPv4 bindings

explanation: DHCPv6 Guard enforces a trust boundary for DHCPv6 server messages (UDP 547/546), blocking rogue DHCPv6 ADVERTISE/REPLY from untrusted access ports (A). RA Guard (B) is essential—but specifically for ICMPv6 Router Advertisements; it does not block DHCPv6 server traffic. DAI (C) is an IPv4 ARP-focused control and does not apply to IPv6. IP Source Guard (D) can enforce source bindings but listed here with IPv4 context; it does not directly stop rogue DHCPv6 servers from issuing configuration. For comprehensive IPv6 protection, combine DHCPv6 Guard with RA Guard and Secure Neighbor Discovery as appropriate.

question: Which network fingerprinting indicator is LEAST likely to be useful for detecting a well-configured, medium-interaction honeypot?

options.A: Inconsistent TCP window scaling, TTL, or timestamp behavior compared to claimed OS.
options.B: Presence of sensor-specific TCP/IP quirks documented in known honeypot fingerprints (e.g., honeyd signature artifacts).
options.C: Shodan/Internet search results showing the IP labeled as “honeypot” or previously flagged.
options.D: DNS PTR records matching the expected enterprise naming convention for critical servers.

explanation: D is correct (least useful) because PTR records can be easily set or spoofed and many enterprises follow inconsistent naming schemes; a matching reverse DNS entry does not reliably prove a host is genuine. A is useful because stack-level inconsistencies are a strong, harder-to-forge indicator. B is useful as many popular honeypot frameworks leave telltale protocol quirks that scanners and fingerprint databases track. C is useful—external reputation/flagging from services like Shodan or past scans supplements active tests; while not definitive alone, such listings are valuable corroboration.

question: During a scheduled patch cycle, the team wants to ensure a recently released web server module patch does not break production. Which countermeasure is the most appropriate operational control to reduce risk before broad deployment?

options.A: Deploy the patch directly to production at midnight to minimize user impact
options.B: Test the patch in a representative staging environment or canary group that mirrors production, then roll out via phased deployment with rollback capability
options.C: Disable monitoring during deployment to avoid false positives from automated checks
options.D: Rely solely on vendor notes that state “no breaking changes” and proceed to patch all systems

explanation: The safe operational control is to first test patches in a staging or canary environment that closely mirrors production, validate functionality and performance, then perform phased rollout with automated rollback strategies (blue/green or canary releases) so issues can be quickly remedied. Option A is risky because immediate production deployment without testing may cause outages even during low-usage windows. Option C is wrong and dangerous—disabling monitoring removes visibility needed to detect regressions. Option D is insufficient because vendor notes may miss environment-specific incompatibilities.

question: The client believes their internet edge blocks “pings,” yet you still need to do safe host discovery for a narrow set of web subnets. Which Nmap host discovery choice provides the MOST precise, low-noise signal under these conditions?

options.A: -PS443 (TCP SYN Ping to 443/tcp on chosen targets)
options.B: -PE -PP (ICMP Echo and Timestamp)
options.C: -Pn (treat all as up)
options.D: -PU53 (UDP “ping” to 53/udp)

explanation: A is correct because a SYN probe to a likely open and permitted service (443/tcp) leverages existing allow-rules to infer liveness with minimal packets; a SYN/ACK indicates likely up without completing a full handshake. B relies on ICMP, which is blocked. C disables discovery altogether and inflates noise by scanning everything, wasting time and increasing detection risk. D to UDP/53 often fails for non-resolvers and can be silently dropped, producing ambiguous results.

question: You need to prepare lures that support elicitation without direct contact whenever possible. Which option is MOST aligned with social-engineering adjacent footprinting while minimizing human interaction?

options.A: Use OSINT to identify public conference talks by staff, then extract tool names, shift patterns, and vendor stacks from recorded sessions to inform later questions
options.B: Send LinkedIn connection requests to staff with a fake recruiter profile to ask about network diagrams
options.C: Submit “lost badge” web forms to prompt HR to call you back and confirm physical access procedures
options.D: Email the CIO requesting a list of privileged groups “for an audit”

explanation: Mining publicly posted talks/panels to harvest non-sensitive operational context is passive and supports better-crafted, minimal-risk elicitation later; it keeps within reconnaissance and respects RoE. B involves deceptive outreach and can escalate quickly beyond footprinting. C manufactures incidents to drive call-backs (active manipulation). D requests sensitive access details (privileged groups) and is out of scope for recon.

question: Which administrative control is MOST effective at reducing successful social-engineering-based footprinting (e.g., elicitation over phone/email) without hindering routine business operations?

options.A: Implement a formal verification/identity protocol for sensitive requests, conduct regular employee training (phishing/vishing simulations), and maintain a least-privilege information disclosure policy with clear escalation paths
options.B: Ban all inbound phone calls and require employees to disable voicemail
options.C: Publish all internal process documents to the public intranet for transparency to reduce unknowns
options.D: Require employees to ignore any caller who asks for information regardless of context

explanation: A is correct because combining procedural authentication (call-back verification, token-based validation), ongoing awareness training and simulations, and a strict minimal-disclosure policy reduces successful social engineering while enabling legitimate requests via vetted channels. B and D are impractical and harm business; they also encourage risky workarounds. C increases leakage and directly enables reconnaissance.

question: You test a search parameter by injecting predicates that should evaluate to TRUE versus FALSE. The TRUE case returns a full product list; the FALSE case returns “0 results.” No delays or error messages are observed. Which SQL injection type are you validating?

options.A: Boolean-based blind (inferential) SQL injection
options.B: Error-based in-band SQL injection
options.C: Out-of-band SQL injection
options.D: Time-based blind (inferential) SQL injection

explanation: Boolean-based blind SQLi infers truth from content differences (e.g., normal list vs empty result) without relying on error text or timing delays, enabling stepwise data extraction through conditional predicates and binary search strategies; this fits the observed “results vs no results” pattern. Option B is incorrect because it requires visible DB error content. Option C is incorrect because it involves secondary exfiltration channels. Option D is incorrect because no artificial delay is used; time-based blind relies on response latency as the signal. Tools like Burp Intruder or sqlmap’s --technique=B are commonly applied in CEH workflows for this case.

question: You want a “push-button” orchestrator on Kali that automates wireless attacks: scanning, WPS PIN/Pixie Dust checks, PMKID harvesting, deauth-handshake capture, and auto-feeding results to cracking utilities. Which tool is designed for this end-to-end automation?

options.A: Kismet
options.B: Wifite
options.C: Eaphammer
options.D: Reaver

explanation: Wifite automates the wireless attack chain: discovery, WPS assessment (with Reaver/Bully and pixiewps where applicable), PMKID requests (via hcxdumptool/hcxtools), deauth-based handshake capture (using aireplay-ng), and preparation of outputs for cracking tools like hashcat—therefore B is correct. A is incorrect because Kismet is a passive sniffer/IDS, not an attack orchestrator. C is incorrect as Eaphammer specializes in evil-twin/enterprise credential attacks (great for PEAP/EAP-TLS social engineering) rather than broad WPS/WPA automation. D is incorrect because Reaver focuses on WPS attacks only and does not provide the full multi-vector automation pipeline.

question: An API accepts JWT bearer tokens without server-side state; logout merely deletes the cookie client-side. After a token is compromised, the attacker can use it until expiration. Which mitigation MOST effectively reduces the practical window for token reuse and allows immediate invalidation?

options.A: Make JWT TTLs longer and rely on client logout flows
options.B: Implement server-side token revocation (denylist) and use short JWT lifetimes with refresh tokens that are rotated and revocable
options.C: Store JWTs in localStorage for easier client management
options.D: Require users to reauthenticate once per week

explanation: Stateless JWTs need complementary server-side controls to support immediate invalidation; implementing a revocation/denylist for jti or session IDs, using short access token lifetimes, and rotating/trackable refresh tokens provides both short exposure windows and a mechanism to revoke compromised tokens promptly. Option A increases risk by lengthening validity. Option C increases exposure to XSS and still does not give the server a revocation mechanism. Option D is policy-level and does not permit immediate revocation after compromise.

question: Which defense-in-depth combination BEST protects against both IP and MAC spoofing attempts that attackers use to enable sniffing (choose the most comprehensive single answer)?

options.A: MACsec on all access links only
options.B: uRPF / BCP38 at the edge plus Port Security on access switches and DHCP snooping + DAI on access VLANs
options.C: Rely exclusively on endpoint host firewalls and antivirus/EDR agents
options.D: Use only static ARP entries on all hosts

explanation: Option B describes a layered approach addressing spoofing at multiple layers: uRPF/BCP38 blocks forged source IPs at the network edge (stopping many reflection/spoof-based attacks), Port Security limits MAC churn and port stealing, and DHCP snooping + DAI validate IP→MAC bindings and block ARP spoofing. Together they mitigate the common L2/L3 vectors used to enable sniffing. MACsec (A) is powerful for confidentiality/integrity on point-to-point links but does not solve DHCP/ARP/Port Security gaps; deploying it everywhere can be impractical. Relying only on host defenses (C) is insufficient because on-path sniffing can capture unencrypted traffic before host controls detect it. Static ARP (D) is unscalable and brittle for large networks and vulnerable to administrative error. CEHv13 best practices emphasize layered network and host controls as in B.

question: A client wants your external port map but insists your real IP must not appear in target logs. Which technique BEST ensures the scan appears to originate from a third-party “zombie” host using predictable IPID behavior?

options.A: Decoy scan (-D) so logs show many IPs and mask yours entirely.
options.B: Spoof all SYNs with a faked source; you’ll still see replies locally.
options.C: Idle scan (-sI <zombie>) leveraging IPID side-channels to make probes appear from the zombie, revealing open/closed states without your IP contacting the target.
options.D: Use proxychains through open HTTP proxies so IDS sees only their IPs.

explanation: Idle scanning is the precise CEHv13 method for origin concealment: it uses a “zombie” with a predictable, low-noise IPID sequence to infer target responses (SYN/ACK vs. RST) via IPID deltas, so the target logs the zombie, not you. Option A (decoys) can still log the real scanner (ordering, TCP nuances, or if the target replies only to the genuine source), and does not guarantee anonymity. Option B fails because without seeing replies to the spoofed IP you cannot complete the scan unless you control/sniff near that IP. Option D proxies your traffic but does not guarantee that intermediate layers won’t leak identifiers; it’s also operationally noisy and detectable.

question: An API you’re documenting returns verbose error messages containing stack traces and full SQL queries when missing required parameters. According to proper footprinting methodology, which remediation and reporting advice is MOST appropriate to include?

options.A: Recommend immediate suppression of detailed server-side error messages in production (return generic error codes/messages), implement parameter validation on the server, and rotate any credentials that may have been exposed; include reproduction reference (cached pages/timestamp) but do not exploit the issue
options.B: Suggest the client enable verbose logging in production so they can better detect exploitation attempts, and provide proof-of-concept exploit code in the report
